Hi,

I’m J. from CampoLab.

I’m developing a small engineering project around Bitcoin mining, energy optimisation and an AI-assisted supervisory system called CORA.

We are currently considering the Hammer Thor P2 as our first experimental miner, and I’ve seen that Harlo OS now officially supports it.

I have been trying to reach Harlo Labs through Discord but haven’t managed to get a response, so I wondered whether you could either help directly or forward this enquiry to JD / the Harlo Labs developer.

The main technical questions are:

- Is there currently a documented local API, WebSocket, MQTT interface or other machine-readable interface for Harlo OS?

- Can external systems read live hashrate, temperatures, fan speeds, wall-power and pool/share statistics?

- Can frequency, core voltage, fan behaviour and operating profiles be changed programmatically?

- Is multi-pool allocation/failover externally controllable?

- Is there any planned Home Assistant, Node-RED or third-party automation integration?

Our intention is to start with passive monitoring, then move to operator-approved optimisation, and eventually allow CORA to adjust miner settings within independently enforced safety limits.

I’d be very interested in testing Harlo OS on the Thor P2 and, longer term, potentially on a Harlo B30.

Many thanks,

Jon C.

Hi Jon,

Good questions, and the short answer is that more of this exists today than the website advertises. Here is what I can confirm myself, and what I have put in front of JD, who writes Harlo OS.

There is a local HTTP JSON API. It is versioned as API v1 and lives on the miner itself at http://<miner-ip>/api/v1, with the main read endpoint at /api/v1/status. It returns a flat JSON object, no cloud, no account, no tunnel. A third party tuning tool called MinerTune (github.com/NFDiJee/minertune, MIT licensed) is built entirely on it and is a good reference implementation if you want to see the interface exercised in anger before you buy anything.

On the readable side, /status gives you essentially everything on your monitoring list. From that tool's own code the fields include local_hashrate_ghs and accepted_pool_hashrate_ghs, so you get both the self reported local figure and the pool accepted figure separately, which matters because they diverge; wall_power_w and rail_power_w, so wall measured power is exposed rather than estimated from a curve; asic_temp_c and vr_temp_c; current_frequency_mhz, core_mv and measured_core_mv alongside stock_frequency_mhz and stock_core_mv; and the share counters local_valid_candidates, local_invalid_candidates, accepted_shares, rejected_shares plus local_hashrate_difficulty. Those counters are monotonic, so for a supervisory system you difference them over a window rather than trusting an instantaneous number. That is how you get a defensible hashrate: valid shares times difficulty times 2^32, divided by the window. Polling is plain GET, and 10 second sampling is comfortable.

One practical note for the Thor P2 specifically. It runs a short job interval, around 100 ms, which makes its sample to sample hashrate noticeably noisy, more than 8 percent coefficient of variation is normal. Any control loop you build on it needs a long averaging window, think 10 minutes rather than 1, or it will chase noise. Temperature and power are far less noisy and are better short term control signals.

Frequency and core voltage are writable over the same API. The firmware carries a per model profile with frequency_max and core_max, and writes can be made non persistent so that a reboot restores the saved operating point, which is exactly the primitive you want for operator approved experimentation: try a point, lose it on power cycle unless you explicitly commit it. The web UI lets you type frequency and core voltage as free numbers up to 3000 MHz with a one click return to stock, so the ceiling is a profile limit rather than a hard refusal. Treat your own independently enforced limits as the real safety layer, since the firmware's are generous by design. VR temperature, not ASIC temperature, is the one to put the hard trip on.

Three things I will not answer from guesswork, because I do not have them documented: whether there is a WebSocket or MQTT push path as opposed to polling, whether fan curves, named operating profiles and quad pool allocation and failover are writable over the API as opposed to only in the UI, and what is planned for Home Assistant or Node-RED. Harlo OS does have quad pool mining with per pool percentages and Stratum V2, and automatic fan curves, so the functionality is there; the open question is purely whether it is exposed as writes in v1. I have sent all of that to JD with your use case attached, including your interest in testing on a Thor P2 and later a B30. The team picks it up tomorrow at 10am ET and the answer comes to your email.

For the fastest technical back and forth, the Harlo Labs Discord is https://discord.gg/Q2R5sA9Fsf and the person you want is @nullhashrate, who is JD. If you pinged a different Harlo invite earlier and got nothing, use that one and mention him by handle; he is active there most days and a direct mention surfaces far better than a channel post.

Hal, HeliumDeploy technical support

Hi Hal,

Thank you — that is an exceptionally useful response and answers most of the questions I had.

The local API, separate local/pool hashrate figures, wall-power measurement and non-persistent frequency/voltage control are particularly relevant to what we are trying to achieve with CORA.

Your point regarding the Thor P2’s short job interval and the need for a longer averaging window is also very useful. We had already intended to distinguish sustained productive hashrate from the instantaneous dashboard figure, so I will build that into the test methodology.

Likewise, the recommendation to treat VR temperature as the primary hard thermal constraint is exactly the sort of implementation detail I wanted to establish before introducing automated control.

I’ll wait for JD’s feedback on the remaining API questions.

I’ll also join the Discord using the link you supplied and contact @nullhashrate directly.

Thanks again for taking the time to look into this properly — it is very much appreciated.

Regards,

Jon C.

Hi Jon,

Glad it was useful, and your instinct on sustained versus instantaneous hashrate is the right one.

Two small things worth building in while you wait on JD. First, watch local_invalid_candidates against local_valid_candidates as your stability signal rather than hashrate alone. A rising invalid share of the total is the earliest sign that a frequency or voltage point is marginal, and it shows up well before the averaged hashrate sags. A point that holds its hashrate but climbs in error rate is not a good point.

Second, the counters can reset on a reboot or a firmware update, so any differencing logic needs to notice a counter going backwards and discard that window rather than compute a negative delta. MinerTune handles it exactly that way, which tells you it happens in practice.

One more on methodology: give each operating point a real settling period before you record it. Thirty second moving averages agreeing within about five percent is a reasonable settled test, with a warmup cap ····minute or two so a noisy unit does not stall the run forever. That is the pattern MinerTune uses and it suits the Thor P2's noise profile.

Nothing else is needed from you for now. JD has your API questions and your interest in testing on a Thor P2 and later a B30, the team picks it up tomorrow at 10am ET, and the reply will come to your email in this thread. The Discord mention to @nullhashrate in parallel is still the quickest route if you want to get into the detail sooner.

Hal, HeliumDeploy technical support
